cards.prompt: A server at `198.51.100.10` runs a plain website on port 80 and a secure website on port 443. A packet arrives for `198.51.100.10:443`. Which program gets it?

options.text: The secure website, because the packet says port 443
The plain website, because every website packet goes to port 80 first
Both website programs, which each keep the parts they need
Whichever website program is less busy at that moment

cards.explanation: The IP address got the packet to the server, and the **port** picks the program: 443 is the secure website's door. Packets don't stop at port 80 first, aren't copied to every program, and never go wherever there's room.

cards.prompt:
Your laptop has two tabs open. `netstat -n` shows:

```
Local Address          Foreign Address
192.168.1.42:51544     198.51.100.10:443
192.168.1.42:51547     203.0.113.80:443
```

A reply arrives at your laptop for port **51547**. Where does it go?

options.text: To the tab talking to 198.51.100.10, because it was opened first
To both tabs, because both are talking to port 443
Back out to a server, because 51547 is a server's port

cards.explanation: 51547 is your laptop's own temporary port for the conversation with `203.0.113.80`, so the reply goes to that tab. Both servers use port 443, which is exactly why your side needs a different temporary port for each conversation.

cards.prompt: A phone opens a TCP connection to a game server to upload a high score. Put the messages in order.
cards.explanation: The phone asks (**SYN**), the server agrees and checks back (**SYN-ACK**), and the phone confirms (**ACK**). Only then is the connection open for the score.

cards.prompt: An online game sends every player's position 30 times a second. A late update is useless, because a newer one is already on its way. Which is the better fit?

options.text: UDP, because it doesn't stop to resend lost updates
TCP, because every single update must arrive
TCP, because the updates must be put back in order
UDP, because it resends lost updates faster than TCP

cards.explanation: When fresh data matters more than complete data, **UDP** fits: a lost update is simply replaced by the next one. TCP would pause to resend the old update, making the game lag. UDP never resends anything.

cards.prompt: Two phones in one home video-call the same server at the same time. Every reply arrives at the router's one public address. How does the router know which phone each reply is for?

options.text: It gave each call its own public port and noted it in its NAT table
The server writes each phone's private address on its replies
It sends every reply to both phones, and each keeps its own
It can't, so only one of the two calls can work at a time

cards.explanation: The router gives each conversation a **different public port** and writes it in its **NAT table**, next to the phone's private address and port. Replies come back to those ports, so each one goes to the right phone. The server never sees the private addresses.

cards.prompt: Match each thing you want to do to the protocol that does it.

pairs.left: Read your inbox on a new laptop
Pass an email between mail servers
Make sure a big download arrives complete

cards.explanation: **IMAP** reads mail kept on a server, **SMTP** sends mail on its way, **DNS** looks up names, and **TCP** resends anything lost, so a download arrives complete.

cards.prompt: A web server receives your request. Like opening a parcel, it takes off the wrappers one at a time. Put them in the order the server opens them, first at the top.

items.label: Ethernet: the wrapper that carried it to this device
TCP: which program, and the pieces in order
HTTP: the request for the page

cards.explanation: The wrappers come off in reverse: **Ethernet** first (outside), then **IP**, then **TCP**, and finally the **HTTP** request itself, the letter at the centre.
